messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Clinical Vignette: Marcus

Marcus was twenty-two when the shelling started. He had been working as a freelance journalist in Eastern Europe, chasing stories that he thought might matter—accounts from ordinary people caught in the crossfire of a conflict that felt distant to Americans but devastatingly real to those living through it. On a March morning, he was interviewing a family in their apartment when the first impact hit the building across the street. The sound was not like anything he had prepared himself for. It was not a noise so much as a physical force that seemed to unmake the world for a moment—a concussive bloom that shattered windows, sent plaster dust into the air like a toxic snow, and left a ringing in his ears that lasted for hours. The family he was with screamed. A child, maybe six years old, was bleeding from a cut on her forehead. Marcus helped them to the bathroom, the safest room, and they huddled there for what felt like hours but was probably only twenty minutes before the bombardment stopped. When he emerged, his hands would not stop shaking.

He stayed in the country for another week, telling himself he was a professional, that this was what he had come for. But the second time the sirens wailed, he felt something break inside him—a certainty that this time he would not survive, that the next shell would find him. He left that night and flew back to the States, arriving in a fog of exhaustion and disbelief at his own fear.

Now, three years later, Marcus works as a salesman for a commercial real estate firm in a mid-sized city. He is functional, or appears to be. He goes to the office most days, meets with clients, closes deals. His girlfriend, Sarah, still loves him, though she has learned not to ask him about his nightmares. But Marcus lives in a state of persistent dread that has become so familiar it feels like the baseline of his existence. What frightened him most was the randomness of it all—the way safety could evaporate in an instant, the way a loud noise could unmake everything. He had come to believe that danger was everywhere, hiding in the ordinary world, waiting. A car backfiring on the street outside his apartment building sends a spike of terror through his chest. The sound of construction equipment, the rumble of trucks, even the sharp slam of a door in the office kitchen—all of these trigger a surge of fear and dread that takes him hours to settle.

At night, the vigilance becomes unbearable. Marcus finds it harder to feel safe after dark, when the world feels more permeable, more vulnerable. He lies awake beside Sarah, listening to every sound in the apartment—the hum of the refrigerator, the creak of the building settling, the distant wail of a siren that could mean anything but which his mind immediately reads as a threat. His concentration at work has suffered. During client presentations, he loses the thread of his own pitch. Colleagues have noticed. His manager pulled him aside last month and asked if everything was okay. Marcus said yes, but the truth is that his mind fractures easily now, scattering whenever there is too much stimulation or whenever something unexpected happens. He feels strong negative emotions—fear that coils in his stomach, anger at his own weakness, guilt that he survived when others did not, shame that he cannot simply move past this. These feelings come without warning and with terrible intensity.

Sarah has suggested therapy more than once. Marcus has resisted, uncertain what talking could possibly change. But last week, after a car alarm went off outside their apartment and he found himself on the floor, heart racing, convinced that something catastrophic was happening, he finally agreed to call someone. He is terrified of what treatment might require of him, terrified that he will never feel safe again, but also desperate for some version of his life back—the person he was before the world revealed itself as fundamentally unsafe.
